I am seventy years old and have farmed this same land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I never went to school, so I cannot read the characters on fertilizer bags, but I know this soil by feel and smell, and I watch what my neighbors do. I have five *mu* of good flat land that my family has worked for generations. I will grow the same double crop as always: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is the backbone of life here. If one crop fails, the other usually saves us.

For the wheat, I will rotary till the ground in early October and sow the improved *shimai* variety that my neighbor Lao Wang recommended—his wheat looked strong last year. I put down about one large bag of compound fertilizer per *mu* before planting, and when the wheat turns yellow at jointing time in spring, I spread another half bag of ammonium bicarbonate. I irrigate three times: once before winter so the seedlings do not freeze, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide two or three times when I see aphids. If the weather is normal I expect about one thousand *jin* per *mu*.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. I plant the maize the same week without tilling—there is only a narrow window before the rains stop. I use hybrid seed, *nongda372*, one small package per *mu*. The maize gets about eighty *jin* of compound fertilizer at planting, and I topdress with a little urea if the leaves look pale. Two irrigations is enough: one when the stalk is knee-high and one before the tassels come out. I spray for weeds and bugs three times in total. Last year I got about eleven hundred *jin* per *mu* of maize, and I hope for the same this year. I do not try new tricks. This system has fed my family for fifty years.
